kg-derivation.title: From E²=p²+m² to a wave operator

questions.q: Applying the standard quantization rules $E \mapsto i\hbar\,\partial_t$ and $\vec p \mapsto -i\hbar\vec\nabla$ to the relativistic relation $E^2 = |\vec p|^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4$ produces which equation (in natural units $\hbar=c=1$)?
choices: $i\,\partial_t\phi = (-\nabla^2 + m^2)\phi$
$(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$, where $\Box = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2$
$\nabla^2\phi = m^2\phi$
questions.hint: Both sides of $E^2=p^2+m^2$ become operators acting on $\phi$; the time derivative comes squared because $E^2$ is on the left.
questions.explain:
Substituting gives $-\partial_t^2\phi = -
abla^2\phi + m^2\phi$, i.e. $(\partial_t^2 - 
abla^2 + m^2)\phi = 0$, which is $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ with the convention $\Box = \partial_t^2 - 
abla^2$. Choice 0 is first-order in time (Schrödinger-like) and is the wrong shape; choice 2 has the wrong sign of $m^2$.

questions.q: Find the error in this derivation: "To get a relativistic Schrödinger equation, take $E = \sqrt{p^2 + m^2}$, apply $E \mapsto i\partial_t$, and obtain $i\partial_t\phi = \sqrt{-\nabla^2 + m^2}\,\phi$. This is the Klein-Gordon equation."
steps: Start from $E = \sqrt{p^2 + m^2}$ (positive square root only).
Identify the resulting equation as the Klein-Gordon equation.
questions.hint: What is the actual Klein-Gordon operator? Is it first-order or second-order in time?
questions.explain:
Step 3 is the error. The equation $i\partial_t\phi = \sqrt{-
abla^2+m^2}\,\phi$ is a valid first-order relativistic equation (sometimes called the 'square-root Klein-Gordon' or relativistic kinetic-energy equation), but it is NOT the Klein-Gordon equation. KG comes from squaring first: $E^2 = p^2 + m^2 \mapsto -\partial_t^2\phi = (-
abla^2 + m^2)\phi$, which is second-order in time and treats the $\pm$ branches symmetrically. The square-root form is non-local in space (the operator $\sqrt{-
abla^2 + m^2}$ has an integral kernel) and is not manifestly Lorentz-invariant in the form written.

questions.q: Why is the Klein-Gordon equation second-order in time, while the Schrödinger equation is first-order?
choices: Because relativistic equations are always second-order; non-relativistic equations are always first-order.
Because $E^2 = p^2 + m^2$ has $E$ squared, while $E = p^2/(2m)$ has $E$ to the first power; canonical quantization preserves the order.
Because $\hbar$ appears squared in KG and to the first power in Schrödinger.
Historical accident — both equations could be written either way.
questions.explain: The relativistic dispersion relation has $E^2$ on one side, so quantization $E \mapsto i\partial_t$ produces $-\partial_t^2$ — second-order in time. The non-relativistic dispersion is linear in $E$, giving $i\partial_t$ — first-order. Choice 0 is wrong (Dirac's equation is first-order and relativistic). Choice 3 is wrong: the order is forced by the structure of the dispersion relation.

questions.q: The Klein-Gordon equation $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ is the relativistic wave equation for a:
choices: spin-1/2 field (Dirac)
spin-0 (scalar) field
spin-1 (vector) field (Maxwell, Proca)
spin-2 (tensor) field (graviton)
questions.hint: $\phi$ is a scalar — one component, transforming trivially under Lorentz rotations.
questions.explain: $\phi$ is a Lorentz scalar (one component, no internal structure under boosts), so KG describes spin-0 fields: pions, kaons, the Higgs. Spin-1/2 needs the 4-component Dirac spinor; spin-1 needs $A^\mu$ with the Maxwell or Proca equation; spin-2 needs $h_{\mu\nu}$. Each higher-spin component, however, individually satisfies KG when spin/gauge structure is turned off.

questions.q: Which of the following are Standard-Model applications of the Klein-Gordon equation? (Select all that apply.)
choices: The free Higgs propagator (kinetic operator $\Box + m_H^2$).
Pions and other spin-0 mesons as effective fields.
Each component of the photon $A^\mu$ in Lorenz gauge ($m=0$ limit).
Free electrons (since they're elementary).
questions.hint: Electrons are spin-1/2 — Dirac, not Klein-Gordon.
questions.explain: The Higgs (0) and pions (1) are scalar fields; their kinetic operator is exactly $\Box + m^2$. Each Lorenz-gauge component $A^\mu$ of the photon satisfies $\Box A^\mu = 0$, the massless KG equation (2). Electrons are spin-1/2 and obey the Dirac equation, not KG — though each component of a Dirac spinor also satisfies $(\Box + m_e^2)\psi_a = 0$ as a consequence.

questions.q: In natural units ($\hbar = c = 1$), what is the Compton wavelength of a Klein-Gordon field with $m = 0.5$? (Round to two decimal places.)
questions.hint: Compton wavelength is $\lambda_C = \hbar/(mc)$, which becomes $1/m$ in natural units.
questions.explain: $\lambda_C = \hbar/(mc) = 1/m$ in natural units. For $m = 0.5$, $\lambda_C = 2.0$. This is the only length scale in the free KG equation — every other dimensional quantity is built from $\lambda_C$ and $c$.

kg-plane-waves.title: Plane-wave solutions and the dispersion relation

questions.q: Substituting the plane wave $\phi = e^{-i(Et - \vec p\cdot\vec x)}$ into $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ produces the dispersion relation. Compute $E$ for $|\vec p| = 2$ and $m = 1$ (positive branch only, in natural units, to three decimal places).
questions.explain: $E_+ = \sqrt{|\vec p|^2 + m^2} = \sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$. This is exactly the relativistic energy-momentum relation $E^2 = p^2 + m^2$ recovered as a dispersion relation.

questions.q: For a Klein-Gordon plane wave with mass $m > 0$ and momentum $\vec p \ne 0$, which is TRUE about the phase velocity $v_\phi = E/|\vec p|$ and group velocity $v_g = dE/d|\vec p|$?
choices: $v_\phi < c$ and $v_g < c$ both — neither exceeds $c$.
$v_\phi > c$ but $v_g < c$ — the phase exceeds $c$ but carries no information; the group stays subluminal.
$v_\phi = v_g$ for any massive plane wave.
$v_\phi < c$ but $v_g > c$ — group velocity is unbounded.
questions.explain: For massive KG: $v_\phi = E/|p| = \sqrt{1 + m^2/p^2} > 1 = c$, while $v_g = |p|/E = |p|/\sqrt{p^2+m^2} < 1$. Their product $v_\phi v_g = 1$. The faster-than-light phase velocity carries no signal (a uniform plane wave conveys no information); only modulations of an envelope do, and those move at $v_g$. Choice 2 holds for massless modes only ($v_\phi = v_g = c$); choice 3 violates causality.

questions.q: Order the steps deriving the Klein-Gordon dispersion relation from a plane-wave ansatz.
items: Read off the dispersion: $E^2 = |\vec p|^2 + m^2$.
Substitute into $(\partial_t^2 - \nabla^2 + m^2)\phi = 0$ to get $(-E^2 + |\vec p|^2 + m^2)\phi = 0$.
questions.hint: Start with the ansatz; end with the dispersion relation.
questions.explain: (3) Posit a plane-wave ansatz. (1) Each derivative pulls down a factor of $-iE$ or $+ip_j$, so the second derivatives produce $-E^2$ and $-|\vec p|^2$. (2) The equation $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ becomes algebraic. (0) For the wave to be non-trivial, the bracket vanishes — this is the dispersion relation.

questions.q: Why can't the negative-energy branch $E_- = -\sqrt{|\vec p|^2+m^2}$ simply be discarded?
choices: Because the equation $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ is second-order in time, so the space of solutions is two-dimensional per momentum mode — both branches are needed for a complete set.
Because the negative energies are required by gauge invariance.
Because Lorentz invariance can be checked only on the negative branch.
Because $E_-$ corresponds to faster-than-light propagation, which is needed for renormalization.
questions.hint: How many initial conditions $(\phi, \partial_t\phi)$ does a second-order PDE in time need?
questions.explain: A second-order PDE in time requires two pieces of initial data per spatial mode: $\phi(0,\vec x)$ and $\partial_t\phi(0,\vec x)$. A general solution must therefore be a linear combination of TWO independent plane waves per momentum, and the natural pair is $E_+$ and $E_-$. Discarding one branch breaks completeness of the Cauchy problem — you can't match arbitrary initial conditions. Choices 1, 2, 3 are nonsense.

questions.q: Under the Feynman-Stückelberg reinterpretation, a negative-energy mode $\phi_-(x) = e^{i(Et - \vec p\cdot\vec x)}$ (with $E > 0$) is read as:
choices: A positive-energy particle moving forward in time with momentum $+\vec p$.
A positive-energy ANTIPARTICLE with reversed 4-momentum: same mass, opposite charge, propagating with $(+E, -\vec p)$ when re-read with time arrow flipped.
A particle that has tunneled through a potential barrier.
A virtual mode that doesn't represent a physical particle.
questions.hint: What sign change converts $e^{i(Et - \vec p\cdot\vec x)}$ to a positive-energy plane wave?
questions.explain: Reading $e^{i(Et - \vec p\cdot\vec x)} = e^{-i(-E)t + i\vec p\cdot\vec x} = (e^{-i(Et + \vec p\cdot\vec x)})^*$ as a positive-energy mode of momentum $-\vec p$ (with charge conjugation built in) is the Stückelberg trick. The result is a positive-energy ANTIPARTICLE with the same mass and opposite charge. After this reinterpretation, the spectrum is bounded below by $+m$ for both species. Distractor 3 confuses this with virtual (off-shell) modes — Stückelberg modes are on-shell; the reinterpretation is about reading the SAME mode two ways.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Feynman-Stückelberg reinterpretation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
choices: It restores a spectrum bounded below by $+m$ for both particles and antiparticles.
It predicts that for a real-valued KG field, particle and antiparticle coincide (e.g. $\pi^0$ is its own antiparticle).
It eliminates the negative-energy branch from the equation.
It generalizes to all spins, not just spin-0 (though Dirac's hole-theory argument got there first for spin-1/2).
questions.hint: Stückelberg keeps the negative branch; he just reads it differently.
questions.explain: (0) After reinterpretation, both species have $E \ge +m$. (1) For a real field, $\phi^* = \phi$, so the creation and annihilation operators coincide and particle = antiparticle — the $\pi^0$, the photon (modulo gauge), and the Higgs (after symmetry breaking, real) are all self-conjugate. (3) Stückelberg's trick works for any spin: a free field of any spin satisfies a wave equation with $\Box + m^2$ in each component, and the same $E_-$ negative-energy issue and same reinterpretation apply. (2) is FALSE: the negative branch is NOT eliminated — it is reread as a positive-energy antiparticle. The equation still has both branches; only the interpretation changes.

kg-current.title: Conserved current and the probability problem

questions.q: The 4-current $j^\mu = i(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi - \phi\,\partial^\mu\phi^*)$ for the Klein-Gordon field satisfies:
choices: $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ (it is conserved) and $j^0 \ge 0$ (positive density).
$\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ but $j^0$ can be negative.
$j^0 \ge 0$ but the current is not conserved.
Neither conserved nor positive-definite.
questions.hint: Multiply the KG equation by $\phi^*$, subtract the conjugate. What does this give? Then check $j^0$ on a sample superposition.
questions.explain: Multiplying $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ by $\phi^*$, subtracting the conjugate, gives $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ — the current is conserved. But $j^0 = i(\phi^*\partial_t\phi - \phi\partial_t\phi^*)$ is NOT positive-definite: a $\phi_+ + \phi_-$ superposition makes it flip sign as in §5's widget. This was the obstacle that forced relativistic wave mechanics to evolve into quantum field theory.

questions.q: What is the modern resolution of the negative-$j^0$ problem in relativistic quantum theory?
choices: Discard the negative-energy modes; this restores positive $j^0$.

Promote $\phi$ to an operator-valued field on Fock space; reinterpret $j^\mu$ as a charge current (particle minus antiparticle number, weighted by $U(1)$ charge), where $j^0 < 0$ just means antiparticle excess.
Replace $j^\mu$ with $|\phi|^2$, which is always positive.
Restrict to real-valued $\phi$ where $j^\mu$ vanishes identically.
questions.hint: QFT replaces the single-particle wavefunction with a quantized field; the conserved current's interpretation changes accordingly.
questions.explain: In QFT $\phi$ becomes an operator with creation/annihilation modes for particles AND antiparticles. The conserved $j^\mu$ acquires a new reading as a charge current: $j^0$ counts particles minus antiparticles times the $U(1)$ charge, and is allowed to be negative when antiparticles dominate. The Schrödinger probability interpretation is recovered only in the non-relativistic limit (§6). Choice 0 breaks the equation (see §4). Choice 2 is dimensionally wrong: $|\phi|^2$ is not a conserved current density. Choice 3 is wrong: real fields have $j^\mu = 0$ only because particle = antiparticle (no $U(1)$ to charge-track), not because the problem disappears.

questions.q: Match each conserved-current interpretation (right) to the setting (left) where it is the correct reading.
left: Klein-Gordon $j^0$ as a charge current in relativistic QFT
Klein-Gordon $j^0$ as a single-particle probability density (pre-QFT)
right: Charge density: signed; negative values mean antiparticle excess.
questions.hint: Probability is non-negative; charge can be either sign; the pre-QFT reading was historically the impasse.
questions.explain: (0) $|\psi|^2$ is the canonical Born density — non-negative, normalized. (1) In QFT $\phi$ is operator-valued and $j^\mu$ becomes a charge current; $j^0 < 0$ just means antiparticles dominate. (2) The pre-QFT attempt to keep $\phi$ as a one-particle wavefunction failed because $j^0$ goes negative on a $\phi_+ + \phi_-$ superposition — the historical impasse that forced the field-theoretic upgrade.

questions.q: Order the steps reducing the Klein-Gordon equation to the free Schrödinger equation in the non-relativistic limit.
items: Write $\phi(t,\vec x) = e^{-imc^2 t/\hbar}\psi(t,\vec x)$ to factor out the rest-energy phase.
Substitute into KG and simplify; obtain $2imc^2\partial_t\psi = -\hbar^2 c^2 \nabla^2\psi - \hbar^2\partial_t^2\psi$.
questions.hint: Start by removing the dominant rest-energy oscillation; end at Schrödinger.
questions.explain: (1) The KG plane wave at rest oscillates as $e^{-imc^2t/\hbar}$; factoring it out leaves the slowly varying $\psi$. (2) Substitution gives a three-term equation. (0) The non-relativistic regime says kinetic energy is much less than rest energy, exactly the parameter that suppresses the second-time-derivative term. (3) Dividing yields free Schrödinger. The negative-energy branch decouples because its $e^{+imc^2t/\hbar}$ factor counter-rotates against the prefactor — its contribution oscillates at $\sim 2mc^2/\hbar$, far above any non-relativistic frequency, and averages to zero.

questions.q: Compare the kinetic energies $E_\text{KG}/m = \sqrt{1 + (p/m)^2} - 1$ and $E_\text{Schr}/m = \tfrac12(p/m)^2$ at $p/m = 0.2$. Compute the relative error $|E_\text{KG} - E_\text{Schr}|/E_\text{Schr}$ as a percentage (one decimal place).
questions.hint: Expand $\sqrt{1+x^2} - 1 \approx \tfrac12 x^2 - \tfrac18 x^4$. The error is $\tfrac18 x^4$ relative to $\tfrac12 x^2$, i.e. $\tfrac14 x^2$.
questions.explain: $E_\text{KG}/m = \sqrt{1.04} - 1 \approx 0.0198$; $E_\text{Schr}/m = 0.02$. Relative error $\approx 0.0002/0.02 = 1\%$ to leading order; the leading correction is $\tfrac14(p/m)^2 = 0.01 = 1\%$. The actual numerical answer is $\approx 1.5\%$ when computed exactly. At low momenta Schrödinger is excellent; the discrepancy grows as $(p/m)^4$ relative to $(p/m)^2$.

questions.q: In which of the following physical settings does the Klein-Gordon equation play a direct role? (Select all that apply.)
choices: Pionic atoms (a $\pi^-$ orbiting a nucleus).
The free Higgs propagator in perturbative QFT (kinetic operator $\Box + m_H^2$).
Free electrons in a semiconductor at room temperature.
Inflaton perturbations on FRW backgrounds in cosmology.
questions.hint: Spin-1/2 → Dirac, not KG. Anything spin-0 and relativistic → KG. Curved-spacetime scalars → KG with a Hubble friction term.
questions.explain: (0) The $\pi^-$ is spin-0; its wavefunction in a Coulomb potential satisfies a KG equation with $V = -Z\alpha/r$. (1) The Higgs propagator in momentum space is $i/(p^2 - m_H^2 + i\epsilon)$, exactly the KG Green's function. (3) The inflaton is a scalar field; perturbations on FRW satisfy a generalized KG equation with a Hubble-friction $3H\dot\phi$ term. (2) Electrons are spin-1/2 → Dirac equation; in a semiconductor, the non-relativistic limit (Schrödinger with effective mass) is ample, but neither is KG.
